pg006_n0006: This textbook contains four chapters: The concept of a map, the Cardinal Directions, Drawing a simple map, and The uses of maps.
pg006_n0007: By learning the contents of this textbook, you will develop the knowledge, skills, and attitude necessary for map drawing, reading, and interpretation.
pg006_n0009: The content of each chapter is presented in the form of text, activities, different maps and diagrams to enable you to develop the intended competencies.
pg006_n0010: Each chapter has sufficient exercises to test your understanding of the specific themes.
pg006_n0011: Therefore, you are advised to do all the exercises and activities in this textbook, along with any additional activities provided by the teacher to develop the intended competencies.

pg007_n0010: The landscape of the earth’s surface varies from one area to another.
pg007_n0011: Normally, it is difficult to understand the landscape of a place without visiting a specific location.
pg007_n0012: The map is a guide that simplifies learning about a certain area on the earth’s surface without having a physical visit to the place.
pg007_n0013: In this chapter, you will learn about the meaning of a map, the types of maps, the essential elements of maps, the characteristics of a good map, and the importance of maps.
pg007_n0014: The competencies developed will enable you to elaborate types of the maps in different contexts.
pg007_n0017: The layout of different places on the earth’s surface
pg007_n0021: A map is a drawing that represents the information found on the earth’s surface by using a specific scale.
pg007_n0022: Maps can be drawn on a paper, a piece of cloth, digital, or any flat area.
pg007_n0023: The geographical information that can be represented on a map includes mountains, valleys, rivers, roads, buildings, and other important information.
pg007_n0024: Maps help us to understand places and how to access them.
pg008_n0005: Explain the difference between a picture and a map.
pg008_n0009: Different criteria are used to identify the types of maps.
pg008_n0010: One of the criteria is the purpose of the map.
pg008_n0011: By using this criterion, there are two types of maps namely; general maps and thematic maps.
pg008_n0015: These are maps that provide general information about a certain area.
pg008_n0016: These maps do not present just one piece of information but offer various details about the area.
pg008_n0017: For example: they can include information about roads, rivers, administrative boundaries, settlements, mountains, and vegetation.
pg008_n0018: These maps help the user to understand the basic information about a place, the relationship between different features presented on the map, and to identify directions on the earth’s surface.
pg008_n0019: Therefore, general maps include: topographical maps, political maps, and road and railway maps.
pg008_n0023: These maps represent the layout of natural and man-made features on the earth’s surface.
pg008_n0024: Also, topographical map use contour lines to show the terrain of an area.
pg008_n0025: Example of natural features include: ocean, lakes, rivers, plains, valleys, mountains, and vegetation.
pg008_n0026: Example of man-made features include buildings, and roads, as presented in Figure 1.
pg008_n0027: These maps are important in planning for construction, tourism, farming, industries, fishing, and business activities.

pg015_n0012: The essential elements of a map are the basic parts that help in the use of a specific map.
pg015_n0013: These elements give the map its meaning and make it accurate.
pg015_n0014: They help to make the map easier to understand and present information about the place correctly.
pg015_n0015: Here are the essential elements that should be included on a map.
pg016_n0002: (a) Frame: a border or outer line surrounding the map.
pg016_n0003: The map frame helps to clearly define the map’s boundaries and separates it from other information on the page.
pg016_n0004: It presents where the map begins and ends;
pg016_n0006: (b) Title: helps to introduce a map to the users by identifies what a map is about or the geographical information or features it represents.
pg016_n0007: For example, if the map presents roads in Tanzania, the title of the map might be Tanzania’s roads map;
pg016_n0009: (c) North Direction: it indicates the direction on the map.
pg016_n0010: It is usually represented by a North arrow.
pg016_n0011: This element helps the reader to identify other directions such as South, East, and West.
pg016_n0012: Knowing directions on a map helps you to understand where things are located;
pg016_n0014: (d) Key: it explains the signs and symbols used on a map.
pg016_n0015: For example, a symbol of a tree might represent a forest, and a blue wavy line might represent a river;
pg016_n0017: (e) Scale: it presents the relationship between the distance on a map and the real distance on the ground.
pg016_n0018: For example, one centimetre on the map might represent ten kilometres on the ground;
pg016_n0020: (f) Grid Lines: these are lines that divide a map into squares.
pg016_n0021: They help to locate specific areas on the map.
pg016_n0022: Each square has a number or letter to help you find things easily; and
pg016_n0024: (g) Source: it presents where the information presented on a map was obtained.
pg016_n0025: The source can be a government organisation, a non-government organisation, or an individual.
pg016_n0026: Presenting the source of the map helps verify its accuracy and allows other users to refer to it in their work.

pg027_n0002: Methods of determining the Cardinal Directions
pg027_n0004: Cardinal Directions of the Earth can be identified using different methods.
pg027_n0005: These methods include using sunrise and sunset, the direction of shadows, the direction of stars, maps, and compasses.
pg027_n0006: At this stage, you will learn how to determine the Cardinal Directions by using sunrise and sunset, the direction of shadow, map and Compass.
pg027_n0008: Determining the Cardinal Directions using the sunrise and sunset
pg027_n0010: Watching the Sun as it rises in the morning or sets in the evening is one way to determine the Cardinal Directions in your location.
pg027_n0011: Normally, the Sunrises in the East and sets in the West.
pg027_n0012: This natural phenomenon helps you identify the East and West directions of your location.
pg027_n0013: By understanding where the sunrises and sunsets, you can gain a basic understanding of the Cardinal Directions.
pg027_n0015: Therefore, in the morning, if you face the sun, you are facing East, and the West will be at your back.
pg027_n0016: To your right side will be South, and to your left side will be North.
pg027_n0017: Similarly, in the evening, if you face the sunset, you are facing the West, and the East will be at your back.
pg027_n0018: To your right side will be North, and to your left side will be South.
pg027_n0020: Determining the Cardinal Directions using the shadow
pg027_n0022: The direction of your shadow in the morning and evening can be used to determine the Cardinal Directions.
pg027_n0023: Usually, when you walk in the morning, the direction of your shadow falls to the West.
pg027_n0024: For example, if you walk while facing the Sun, your shadow will be behind you, and if you walk while the Sun is to your back, your shadow will be in front of you, thus the direction will be West.
pg027_n0025: Similarly, in the evening, the direction of your shadow will be East, as presented in Figure 2.

pg030_n0018: A compass is a device used to identify the North direction.
pg030_n0019: There are two types of compasses, namely: digital compass and analog compass.
pg030_n0020: A digital compass uses technology to detect and display the North direction.
pg030_n0021: This type of compass is often integrated into GPS, modern watches, smartphones, and transport vehicles such as cars, boats, and planes, as presented in Figure 4.

pg031_n0020: The intercardinal directions are points that lie between the Cardinal Directions.

pg031_n0023: They offer more detailed explanations or specific directions, leading to a more precise and accurate understanding of a location.
pg031_n0024: Intercardinal directions are commonly used in various fields, such as aviation, maritime navigation, geography, and weather forecasting.

pg038_n0020: Map drawing is the art and science of representing the locations of features on the earth’s surface on paper or any flat surface.
pg038_n0021: The study of map drawing is called cartography, and a person who draws maps is called a cartographer.
pg038_n0022: In map drawing, symbols are used to represent features such as roads, houses, rivers, and mountains.
pg038_n0023: This process emphasizes maintaining the correct proportions between the area, real objects, and the symbols placed on the map.
pg038_n0025: Features that can be presented on a map
pg038_n0027: Maps can display various features depending on their purpose.
pg038_n0028: For example, a map can present roads that lead to different places, buildings
pg039_n0002: like houses and schools, and rivers and oceans to represent water bodies.
pg039_n0003: Also, maps can present mountains and valleys to represent higher and lower land, green areas like national parks and forests, city or country boundaries, and sports fields.
pg039_n0005: However, not everything on the earth’s surface will be presented on a map.
pg039_n0006: The features included on a map are those which are important to the map users.
pg039_n0007: The cartographer decides what to include on the map based on the needs of the map users.
pg039_n0008: Therefore, maps present only the key features necessary to make them easy to read and understand.

pg042_n0004: A map scale is the ratio between the distance on the map and the real distance on the ground.
pg042_n0005: The scale helps to show how the measurements on the map correspond to real-world measurements.
pg042_n0006: The scale can be presented as a statement, representative fraction or ratio and linear scale.

pg042_n0011: For example, one centimetre on the map represents one kilometre on the ground.

pg060_n0008: In life, sometimes we need to travel from one place to another that we are not familiar with, to access services, relax, or visit relatives and friends.
pg060_n0009: It can be difficult to reach the intended place if we do not have someone to guide us.
pg060_n0010: However, a map is a useful tool that can help you to find the route and guide you to your destination.

pg081_n0013: Using maps to identify Earth’s relief
pg081_n0015: Relief refers to the elevation of the land including mountains, valley, hills, plains and plateaus.
pg081_n0016: Maps use different symbols and colours to represent the Earth’s relief.
pg081_n0017: For example, contour lines on a map are used to indicate ground elevation or depression of the land.
pg082_n0004: Often, mountains and hills are presented with brown or red colours or contour lines.
pg082_n0005: The darker the colour, the higher the mountain.
pg082_n0006: Or, if the contour lines are too close, it means the land is steep, like a mountain.
pg082_n0007: Hills, which are smaller than mountains, are usually indicated with lighter brown or green colours or by close contour lines.
pg082_n0011: Valleys are the low areas between mountains or hills.
pg082_n0012: On a map they can be presented with green colours or inward-curving contour lines.
pg082_n0013: Plains, which are flat areas, are often represented with green colours.
pg082_n0014: Also, they can be represented with contour lines.
pg082_n0015: If the lines are far apart, it means that the land is flat.
pg082_n0019: These are flat areas on top of high land, usually presented with brown colours.
pg082_n0020: Also on a map, a plateau can be presented by contour lines that are close on the sides and spread out on top.
pg082_n0021: The spread-out lines show the flat part of the plateau.
pg082_n0023: Generally, when using a map to identify relief of a certain area, pay attention to the colours or contour lines.
pg082_n0024: Understanding the relief of the land is useful for various purposes, such as planning where to build, and learning about the environment.

pg083_n0015: Using maps to determine the distribution of features and people
pg083_n0018: Use books or online reliable sources to learn how the distribution of people and objects are represented on a map.

pg084_n0002: Maps are essential tools for identifying where people live and where different features are found.
pg084_n0003: Maps can use dot symbols, or colours to present the distribution of people.
pg084_n0004: For example, if you know that many dots are close together on a map, it means many people live in that area, like in big cities.
pg084_n0005: If the dots are spread out, it means fewer people live there, like in the village or small towns.
pg084_n0007: The distribution of people and objects also can be determined by using Geographic Information Systems (GIS) and other digital tools.
pg084_n0008: This helps us to understand where people are more or less crowded.
pg084_n0010: Maps also use specific symbols to represent the distribution of different features on the earth’s surface.
pg084_n0011: For example, a house symbol presents the locations of homes, while a school symbol presents the locations of schools.
pg084_n0012: Similarly, maps use different colours to present features.
pg084_n0013: For example, blue might be used for water sources like rivers and lakes, green for areas with forests, and yellow for desert areas.
pg084_n0015: Generally, you are advised to use the key to know which symbols or colours are used to represent the distribution of objects and people so that you can use the map properly.

Relief means the height and shape of the land.
It includes:
- mountains
- valleys
- hills
- plains
- plateaus
pg081_n0016_easy_read: Maps use different symbols and colours to show the Earth's relief.
pg081_n0017_easy_read: For example, contour lines on a map show where the land is high or low.
pg082_n0004_easy_read: Maps often present mountains and hills with brown or red colours, or with contour lines.
pg082_n0005_easy_read: The darker the colour, the higher the mountain is.
pg082_n0006_easy_read: If the contour lines are very close together, it means the land is steep, like a mountain.
pg082_n0007_easy_read:
Hills are smaller than mountains.
Maps usually show hills with lighter brown or green colours, or with close contour lines.
pg082_n0011_easy_read: Valleys are low areas between mountains or hills.
pg082_n0012_easy_read: On a map, valleys can be presented with green colours or inward-curving contour lines.
pg082_n0013_easy_read:
Plains are flat areas.
Maps often show plains with green colours.
pg082_n0014_easy_read: Maps can also show plains with contour lines.
pg082_n0015_easy_read: If the lines are far apart, it means the land is flat.
pg082_n0019_easy_read:
Plateaus are flat areas on top of high land.
Maps usually present them with brown colours.
pg082_n0020_easy_read: On a map, a plateau can also be presented with contour lines that are close on the sides and spread out on top.
pg082_n0021_easy_read: The spread-out lines show the flat part of the plateau.
pg082_n0023_easy_read: In general, when you use a map to identify the relief of an area, look at the colours or contour lines.
pg082_n0024_easy_read: Understanding the relief of the land is useful for different purposes, such as planning where to build and learning about the environment.
